paras: The lynching of Cato Garrett took place on July 7, 1903, when masked men stopped a passenger train at Stout's Crossing, a flag station south of Vicksburg, Mississippi, took Garrett, a 17-year-old Black youth, from the officer escorting him, and hanged him from a bridge. A special grand jury had indicted him that morning for the killing of Harry Stout, a white farmer, and he was being returned to Vicksburg for trial. The Associated Press carried the story nationally, and the Seattle Republican, a Black weekly, later entered Garrett's name in a list of the year's lynchings headed "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign."

According to an Associated Press dispatch from Vicksburg dated July 4, Garrett killed Stout, "a well-known white farmer," about four miles south of the city that day after a quarrel about a horse. That first bulletin said Garrett shot Stout; every later account said he stabbed him. Garrett was jailed in Vicksburg amid what the dispatch called "very strong" feeling and fears of a lynching.

On the morning of July 4, according to a Vicksburg report in the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, a crowd gathered at the jail about 10 o'clock and demanded the prisoner. Sheriff Brennan and four deputies armed with Winchester rifles rushed Garrett onto an outgoing train as the crowd came within sight of the depot, and he was taken to Monroe, Louisiana, and then to Natchez.

On July 7 a grand jury, which the Times-Promoter of Hernando said Judge Anderson had specially convened to give Garrett "a hasty trial," returned an indictment. Brennan asked the Adams County sheriff to send Garrett back, and he set out with an officer named Paul on the afternoon train due in Vicksburg at 5 o'clock. As the train neared Stout's Crossing, the Times-Promoter reported, Garrett cried out that this was where he had killed Stout and that his brother was plowing in the field.

At the crossing armed, masked men stopped the train; in the Associated Press account half of them held the crew while the rest took Garrett from the smoking car. He was praying as he was taken off, a noose already around his neck, and was hanged from a country-road bridge east of the railroad near where Stout had died, without a shot fired. At the Vicksburg depot, where Brennan and a posse waited, Paul reported that the men were masked and carried revolvers and that he had been unable to resist.

The Times-Promoter attributed the lynching to "the close friends of the murdered man," who it said wanted "quicker justice" than the hastened trial. No report of an inquest or of arrests appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press account ran on July 8 from Savannah and Montgomery to St. Louis, Indianapolis and Minneapolis under headlines such as "Lynched the Slayer of Harry Stout" and "Mob Held Up the Train." A second Vicksburg dispatch, printed by the Washington Times and more fully by the Times-Promoter, supplied Garrett's age, the noose and the prayer. Weekly digests in four states shrank the story to a sentence or a paragraph, and a Minnesota year-end list in January 1904 recorded it as a lynching "for stabbing Harry Stout to death."

White papers stated the accusation as fact, calling Garrett "the slayer of Harry Stout" and placing the hanging "near the scene of his crime." The Times-Promoter headed its account "Jerked Into Eternity" and "Cato Garrett Pays the Penalty for His Foul Deed," and the Hattiesburg paper wrote that the men acted "as though it was a stern but unpleasant duty."

The only Black-press notice found is the Seattle Republican's August 7 list, which entered "Cato Garrett, Negro, Stout's Crossing, Miss." under July 7 without any account of the accusation. The paper introduced the list as "Uncle Sam's" lynching record, a "pen picture" that Russia and Turkey might emulate if they wished to "do away with the Christians living among them."

The two Vicksburg dispatches disagree on the size of the mob: the Washington Times and the Times-Promoter gave fifteen men, the Associated Press fifty. The crossing's distance from Vicksburg is given as four miles by the Times-Promoter, five by the Osceola Times and six by the Associated Press.

framing.detail: Times-Promoter headlines 'Jerked Into Eternity' and 'Cato Garrett Pays the Penalty for His Foul Deed', and says Stout's friends wanted 'quicker justice'.
Hattiesburg Daily Progress calls Garrett 'the slayer of Harry Stout' and says the men went about the hanging 'as though it was a stern but unpleasant duty'.

AP text ran under headlines such as 'Lynched the Slayer of Harry Stout', 'Mob Held Up the Train' and 'Negko Murderer Lynched', treating the accusation as fact ('the negro who stabbed Harry Stout to death').
Port Gibson Reveille's 'Killing and Lynching' and Portland's 'Another Negro Hanging' are bare two-sentence items.
Seattle Republican's 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign' offers the list as a 'pen picture' Russia and Turkey might emulate to 'do away with the Christians living among them'.

'Evans' appears only in Northern reprints of one wire version; the local and first reports say Stout, and the crossing bears that name.
The Hattiesburg account describes the crowd gathering at the jail about 10 o'clock and an immediate departure by train, via Monroe, La.
